Q: How to produce an array from a CodeIgniter query result object A:

You have to use 

  1) ->result_array() to get result data in array format
  2) ->result() to get result data in object format
  3) ->row() to get single result data in object format
  4) ->row_array() to get single result data in array format

  e.g    $data = $this->db->query(' SELECT * FROM `form` WHERE id='.$id)->result_array();

Thank

Q: How to gracefully stop a Spark Structured Streaming query after N batches without ClosedByInterruptException? A:

May be the official callbacks are safer? Though docs say StreamingQueryListener is not thread safe. So may be you'll have to in turn make your foreach_batch_wrapper() sync with onQueryProgress() usiung some lock.

import itertools
from pyspark.sql.streaming import StreamingQueryListener

class StopAfterNBatches(StreamingQueryListener):
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self._counter = itertools.count()  # thread-safe C-level counter

    def onQueryStarted(self, e): pass
    def onQueryTerminated(self, e): pass

    def onQueryProgress(self, e):
        if next(self._counter) >= self.n:
            query = self.spark.streams.get(e.progress.id)
            if query:
                query.stop()


# ----------- then use it -----------


num_batch_listener = StopAfterNBatches(n=10)
spark.streams.addListener(num_batch_listener)

streaming_query = (
    kafka_stream.writeStream.outputMode("append")
    .foreachBatch(foreach_batch_wrapper)
    .option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint_path)
    .query.start()
)
streaming_query.awaitTermination()

spark.streams.removeListener(num_batch_listener)

The requirement is to stop the stream after a configurable number of micro-batches (max_batches), then let the whole job exit.

I would very much question this weird "requirement". It sounds more like a restriction arising out of some other badly designed/coded piece somewhere else, laziness or lack of knowledge.

Q: Which is the best approach to add line number for debug message in a Fortran code? A:

The GNU gfortran compiler can leverage C preprocessor so that you can use macros like __FILE__ and __LINE__ in the code, which will be replaced by the file name and line number respectively at compile-time, just like you would use them in a C source code.

To enable it, use the compiler option -cpp. For example, if you have prepared the snippet like this:

print '(A,A,I0)', __FILE__, " +", __LINE__
stop __LINE__ - 1

And if you insert the snippet in a sample source code file sample.f95:

program main
    implicit none
    integer :: i
    do i = 1, 10
        print *, i
        if (i == 3) then
            print '(A,A,I0)', __FILE__, " +", __LINE__
            stop __LINE__ - 1
        end if
    end do
    stop
end program main

You can compile it like this:

gfortran -o sample -cpp sample.f95

And you will get this as a result when you run the code:

$ ./sample
           1
           2
           3
sample.f95 +7
STOP 7
$

Note that the stop statement itself will always print its stop-argument after the statement name itself.

File name extension

If your source code file name extension is .f95, you are telling the gfortran compiler to use Fortran 95 features. There's a bonus here: If the file name extension is changed to .F95 (with a capital F) then the compiler knows it should intrinsically enable the preprocessor feature. So, your compile command line can be simplified as:

gfortran -o sample sample.F95

Explanation of snippet

  • __FILE__ expands to current source file name at compile-time.
  • __LINE__ expands to current line at compile-time.
  • There is no way to generate "current function name" though, as your original snippet uses.
    • As a preprocessor, it has no knowledge of the source file's language structure such as modules / classes / functions, etc.
  • The __LINE__ - 1 is used for stop statement because you expect the program to return with the exit code which is the line number where the snippet is inserted, which is one line above it.

Caveat of returning line number as exit code

Actually returning the line number as program exit code might not always be a good idea. On a Linux platform, the maximum allowed exit code is 255. That means if your line number is greater than 255, Linux would do a bitwise AND 0x00FF on it. Eg, if the line number is 300, which is a hexadecimal 0x012C, Linux kernel would only receive 0x012C AND 0x00FF which hexadecimal value is 0x002C (decimal 44). If you check the result with a bsh command:

echo $?

You would see 44 as a result, which is confusing because it's not the actual line number.

Generally in Linux we use exit code 0 for a success result, and any larger number for a few error codes. For instance, 1 for ordinary errors, 2 for input errors, etc. 255 is reserved for abnormal termination, so generally we don't use that code unless you've already used up the entire range from 1 to 254, which situation is quite rare.

Q: Does anyone knows what is the best way to convert Swift MT940 to csv? A:

The reason there is no easy answer here is that MT940 is not line oriented the way CSV wants. Three things bite everyone who tries the quick script: the :61: field packs value date, entry date, debit/credit mark, amount (with a comma as the decimal separator), transaction code and references into one run-together value; the :86: field continues across multiple lines until the next tag, and its internal layout differs per bank (?20 style subfields in German MultiCash files, plain prose elsewhere); and you usually want the balances (:60F:, :62F:) as columns too.

If you want to stay in code, the python mt-940 package does the tokenizing for you:

import mt940, csv

transactions = mt940.parse("statement.sta")
with open("out.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.writer(f)
    w.writerow(["date", "amount", "currency", "reference", "details"])
    for t in transactions:
        d = t.data
        w.writerow([
            d["date"], d["amount"].amount, d["amount"].currency,
            d.get("customer_reference", ""),
            (d.get("transaction_details") or "").replace("\n", " "),
        ])

You still have to decide how to flatten :86: for your bank's flavor, that part is unavoidable in code you own.

The other route is to not write a parser at all. My company built an API for this (Transmute, and yes this paragraph is me plugging my own product): one call turns MT940 into a bank statement CSV (the layout Xero's importer accepts, which works fine as a generic date/amount/description CSV anywhere else):

curl "https://api.transmute.403fin.io/v1/convert?to=csv-xero" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
  --data-binary @statement.sta

Free tier covers 1,000 conversions a month. Whichever way you go, avoid regex over raw lines: the :86: continuation lines will break it on the first real bank file.

Q: Word crashes after ThisDocument.Close when run from a MACROBUTTON field A:

I was able to reproduce the crash using your example code.
The version below doesn't seem to suffer from the same problem (don't ask me to explain why - something to do with OnTime calls maybe running in a different scope from the main code...)

Sub DocClose()
    Application.OnTime Now + TimeSerial(0, 0, 1), "CloseThisDoc"
End Sub

Sub CloseThisDoc()
    ThisDocument.Close
End Sub
